title: How Often Should HVAC Air Filters Be Changed?
h1: How Often Should You Change Your HVAC Air Filter?
description: Most HVAC filters need changing every 1 to 3 months, depending on filter type, pets, allergies and smoke. Here's how to set the right schedule for your home.
quick_answer: Check your HVAC filter every month and change it every one to three months for most standard one-inch filters. Change it more often if you have pets, allergies or heavy dust, and during wildfire smoke. Thicker four- or five-inch media filters can usually last six months or more. If it looks gray and clogged, replace it.
body:
Why does the filter schedule matter?

The filter is the system's first line of defense. It catches dust, hair and pollen before they reach the blower, the coil and your ducts. When it fills up, airflow drops and the system has to work harder to move air through the house.

A clogged filter can freeze an AC coil, overheat a furnace and trip its safety switch, and push dust around the filter edges into the ductwork. Many no-heat and no-cool calls start with a filter that hasn't been changed in a long time.

How long do different filters last?

Filter life depends on its thickness and material. Use these as starting points, then adjust based on what you see:

Filter typeTypical change interval
Thin fiberglass (1 inch)Every month
Pleated (1 inch)Every 1 to 3 months
Pleated (2 inch)Every 2 to 4 months
Media filter (4 to 5 inch)Every 6 to 12 months
Washable filterRinse every month, replace when damaged

The manufacturer's guidance on the filter box or cabinet is the best reference for your exact filter.

What should make you change it sooner?

  • Pets. Dogs and cats shed constantly, and hair builds up fast on the filter.
  • Allergies or asthma. A fresh filter catches more of what triggers symptoms.
  • Wildfire smoke. Check the filter daily during smoke events and swap it as soon as it darkens.
  • Santa Ana winds. Dry wind pushes fine dust into the house, so look at the filter after a windy stretch.
  • Remodeling. Construction dust can clog a filter in days.
  • Heavy use. Inland homes running the AC hard through summer move far more air than a coastal home with the windows open.

How can you tell when a filter is dirty?

Pull it out and hold it up to a light. If you can barely see light through it, or the surface is gray and covered in a layer of dust and hair, it's done. Other signs include weaker airflow from the vents, more dust on furniture, and the system running longer than usual to reach the set temperature.

Set a reminder on your phone for the first of each month to check it. It takes less than a minute, and you'll quickly learn how fast your home loads a filter.

Does a higher MERV rating mean changing it more often?

Often, yes. MERV ratings describe how well a filter catches small particles. A higher MERV filter traps more, which means it can load up faster and restrict airflow sooner. That's fine as long as your system can handle it and you replace it on time.

Not every system is designed for a dense filter. If you want better filtration for allergies or smoke, ask a technician whether your blower can handle it or whether a thicker media cabinet would be a better fit. Our indoor air quality service covers filter upgrades and media cabinets.

Where is the filter in a Southern California home?

Most homes here don't have basements, so filters are usually in one of these places:

  • A large return grille in a hallway ceiling or wall
  • Inside or next to the furnace in a hall closet
  • At the furnace in the garage
  • At the air handler in the attic, which is easy to forget

Some homes have more than one return, each with its own filter. If you're not sure where yours are, a technician can show you during your next tune-up.

What's the right way to buy replacement filters?

Write down the exact size printed on the frame of your current filter, such as 16x25x1, and buy that size. A filter that's even a little too small leaves a gap, and dusty air will take the easy path around it. Keep a few spares on hand so you're not tempted to leave a dirty one in place until the next trip to the store.

When you swap it, note the date on the frame with a marker. Next month, you'll know exactly how long it has been in and how fast it loaded up.
faqs: What happens if I never change my HVAC filter?
Airflow drops, the system runs longer, and dust gets pushed into the coil and ducts. Over time a clogged filter can freeze the AC coil, overheat the furnace and shorten the life of the blower motor.
Is a more expensive filter always better?
Not always. Higher-efficiency filters catch more particles, but some systems aren't built for the extra resistance. Choose the highest rating your system handles well, and change it on schedule.
Do I need to change my filter if I don't run the system much?
Yes, check it anyway. Filters still collect dust over time, and coastal homes that rarely use the AC can still get musty filters. Check monthly and change when it looks dirty.
Which way does the filter go in?
Look for the arrow printed on the frame. It should point toward the furnace or air handler, in the direction the air is moving.
